title: async/await vs Threads
oneLiner: What await really does, why it lets a few threads serve thousands of I/O-bound requests, and why it does nothing for CPU-bound work.
keyTakeaway: await does not start a thread. It registers the rest of the method as a continuation, returns the thread to its caller (ultimately the thread pool, a set of reusable worker threads), and resumes the method on a pool thread when the awaited operation finishes. That frees threads during I/O waits, so async multiplies throughput for I/O-bound work. For CPU-bound work there is no waiting to free up: you need more cores, via Task.Run or Parallel.For, not await.
explanation:
Work is either CPU-bound (the thread is busy computing: hashing, resizing images, parsing a big file already in memory) or I/O-bound (the thread is waiting for something outside the CPU: a database, an HTTP call, a disk read). A typical web request is overwhelmingly I/O-bound: a millisecond of CPU and tens of milliseconds waiting on the database.

With synchronous code, a thread that calls the database sits blocked for the whole wait, holding its stack and doing nothing. A server with 4 pool threads and 10 requests in flight serves 4 at a time; the other 6 queue up even though the CPU is almost idle. The thread pool will slowly add threads when it sees this, which is the thread pool starvation you get from blocking calls such as .Result and .Wait() inside async code.

await changes what happens during the wait. The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine. The method runs synchronously, on the caller's thread, until it reaches an await on a task that has not completed yet. At that point it stores its local variables in the state machine object (on the heap), registers "run the rest of me" as a continuation on that task, and returns an incomplete Task to its caller. The thread is now free to serve another request. The I/O itself is carried out by the OS and the network card; no thread sits waiting for it (on Windows it completes through an I/O completion port, on Linux through epoll). When the result arrives, the continuation is queued to the thread pool and some pool thread, not necessarily the original one, resumes the method right after the await.

That is why async helps only I/O-bound work. If a request is 8 ms of computation, there is no wait to release the thread during, and await on a CPU-bound task just moves the same work to another thread. CPU-bound throughput is capped by the number of cores; to use more of them, split the work with Task.Run, Parallel.For or PLINQ. In a UI app, Task.Run is also how you keep heavy computation off the UI thread.

Pitfalls interviewers like: blocking on async code with .Result or .Wait() wastes a thread and, where there is a SynchronizationContext (WinForms, WPF, old ASP.NET), can deadlock, because the continuation needs the very thread that is blocked waiting for it. ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so there it "only" starves the pool. async void cannot be awaited and its exceptions crash the process; use it only for event handlers. Await several independent calls together with Task.WhenAll rather than one after another. ConfigureAwait(false) tells a library not to resume on the captured context. And async is not parallel by itself: one async method awaiting three calls in sequence still does them one at a time.
